name: Ojeda and Vespucci to Venezuela
traveler: Alonso de Ojeda, Juan de la Cosa and Amerigo Vespucci
summary: Licensed to follow up Columbus's third voyage, Alonso de Ojeda sails with the pilot Juan de la Cosa and the Florentine Amerigo Vespucci. Vespucci's ships break away south-east along the Guiana coast, perhaps as far as the mouths of the Amazon, before the fleet follows the Caribbean shore of South America and names a village on stilts Little Venice: Venezuela. Juan de la Cosa drew what they saw into his world map of 1500, the first to show the Americas.

stops.note: Four ships sail from the bay of Cádiz.
Water and supplies before the crossing.
Landfall on a low coast of mangroves after twenty-four days at sea. Here Vespucci's ships part from Ojeda's and turn south-east.
Vespucci writes of great rivers whose fresh water ran far out to sea. Whether he got this far is disputed; Vicente Yáñez Pinzón certainly did, in January 1500.
Back north-west past the mouths of the Orinoco, into the gulf Columbus had found the year before.
They call it the Island of Giants, for the tall people they meet there.
A village of houses on stilts over the water reminds them of Venice, and they call the place Venezuela, Little Venice.
The westernmost point they reach, on the Guajira peninsula.
They put in on Hispaniola, to the anger of Columbus, who held the island's trade as his own.
Home with pearls and some two hundred captives, sold as slaves.
